🧭 Abdominal Abscess

Abdominal abscess is a localized collection of pus or infected fluid. The central radiology task is to recognize a discrete drainable collection, distinguish it from phlegmon and sterile postoperative fluid, identify the source, and determine whether image-guided drainage is appropriate.
Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis.

📚 Summary
  • Typical CT pattern: loculated or encapsulated low-density fluid collection with peripheral rim enhancement, with or without gas.
  • Internal gas is highly suspicious for infection when there has been no recent intervention, but gas may also reflect bowel communication.
  • Absence of gas does not exclude abscess; RadPrimer states that about half of abscesses contain gas.
  • Inflammatory support findings include adjacent fat stranding, edema, fascial thickening, and low-density parenchymal edema around intraparenchymal abscesses.
  • Use the term abscess for a discrete drainable collection; ill-defined inflammatory phlegmon is not equivalent to a drainable abscess.

🖼️ Key Imaging Findings
CT
  • Best overall imaging tool is contrast-enhanced CT.
  • Contents may have simple-fluid attenuation or be mildly hyperdense; rim enhancement and surrounding inflammatory change are major clues.
  • Hepatic pyogenic abscess may mimic metastasis as a ring-enhancing mass; reactive perilesional hyperenhancement may occur.
MR Imaging
  • Central fluid is low on T1 and high on T2, with peripheral rim enhancement; restricted diffusion with low ADC is often present.
  • Fat-saturated sequences can make surrounding edema conspicuous.
Ultrasound
  • Complex fluid may contain low-level echoes, debris, membranes, or septations; the center is avascular with peripheral hyperemia.
  • Gas may produce echogenic foci with ring-down artifact or dirty posterior acoustic shadowing.
  • In hepatic infection, an ill-defined altered-echogenicity phlegmon can evolve into a well-defined hypoechoic mature abscess with internal echoes.
Nuclear Medicine
  • Source-listed options include labeled white blood cell imaging, gallium, and FDG PET; FDG PET is sensitive but nonspecific.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Postoperative lymphocele: simple fluid along lymphatic pathways near clips, without enhancing rim or gas.
  • Biloma: collection near the biliary tree after biliary or hepatic surgery; usually simple unless infected.
  • Postoperative seroma: simple fluid that may contain recent postoperative gas and may require clinical correlation to distinguish from abscess.
  • Loculated ascites: minimal mass effect, no rim enhancement, and no internal gas.
  • Pancreatic pseudocyst: pancreatitis history or stigmata; pseudocapsule develops over weeks.
  • Hematoma: attenuation varies with age; acute clot is often high attenuation.
  • Retained oxidized cellulose (Surgicel): postoperative gas with little fluid and no discrete drainable collection.
  • Cystic or necrotic neoplasm can mimic abscess, especially when infectious clinical findings are absent.

🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Etiologies include enteric perforation, postoperative infection, bacteremia, and trauma.
  • RadPrimer describes pus within a peripheral fibrocapillary capsule; enteric abscesses are often polymicrobial.
  • Core notes that hepatic abscess commonly arises from bowel processes such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, Crohn disease, or bowel surgery; E. coli is the most common causative organism in that hepatic context.
  • Core also notes that perforated appendicitis can progress to abscess and that diverticulitis is complicated when abscess is present.

🛠️ Drainage / Management Pivots
  • Ideal percutaneous target: well-defined, encapsulated, fluid-filled abscess >3 cm with a safe catheter route.
  • Small abscesses, usually <3 cm, may be treated with antibiotics alone.
  • RadPrimer reports approximately 80% success for percutaneous abscess drainage with proper patient selection.
  • CT or ultrasound can guide transcutaneous, transgluteal, transrectal, or transvaginal drainage.
  • Most drain in 10-14 days; complex multiseptated collections or enteric fistulas may require weeks to months.
  • Catheter removal may be considered when output is <10 cc per shift or the cavity resolves on imaging.

⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • In postoperative patients, infected and noninfected collections can overlap; symptoms, labs, aspiration, timing, and follow-up may be required.
  • Do not require gas for diagnosis and do not label nondrainable phlegmon as abscess.
  • Gas after surgery is not automatically infection: Surgicel is a source-supported mimic.
  • Failure of presumed abscess drainage should raise concern for a cystic or necrotic neoplasm, as shown by the GIST mimic cases.

Abdominal abscess is a localized collection of pus or infected fluid. The central radiology task is to recognize a discrete drainable collection, distinguish it from phlegmon and sterile postoperative fluid, identify the source, and determine whether image-guided drainage is appropriate.
Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis.

📚 Summary
  • Typical CT pattern: loculated or encapsulated low-density fluid collection with peripheral rim enhancement, with or without gas.
  • Internal gas is highly suspicious for infection when there has been no recent intervention, but gas may also reflect bowel communication.
  • Absence of gas does not exclude abscess; RadPrimer states that about half of abscesses contain gas.
  • Inflammatory support findings include adjacent fat stranding, edema, fascial thickening, and low-density parenchymal edema around intraparenchymal abscesses.
  • Use the term abscess for a discrete drainable collection; ill-defined inflammatory phlegmon is not equivalent to a drainable abscess.

🖼️ Key Imaging Findings
CT
  • Best overall imaging tool is contrast-enhanced CT.
  • Contents may have simple-fluid attenuation or be mildly hyperdense; rim enhancement and surrounding inflammatory change are major clues.
  • Hepatic pyogenic abscess may mimic metastasis as a ring-enhancing mass; reactive perilesional hyperenhancement may occur.
MR Imaging
  • Central fluid is low on T1 and high on T2, with peripheral rim enhancement; restricted diffusion with low ADC is often present.
  • Fat-saturated sequences can make surrounding edema conspicuous.
Ultrasound
  • Complex fluid may contain low-level echoes, debris, membranes, or septations; the center is avascular with peripheral hyperemia.
  • Gas may produce echogenic foci with ring-down artifact or dirty posterior acoustic shadowing.
  • In hepatic infection, an ill-defined altered-echogenicity phlegmon can evolve into a well-defined hypoechoic mature abscess with internal echoes.
Nuclear Medicine
  • Source-listed options include labeled white blood cell imaging, gallium, and FDG PET; FDG PET is sensitive but nonspecific.

⚖️ Differential Diagnosis
  • Postoperative lymphocele: simple fluid along lymphatic pathways near clips, without enhancing rim or gas.
  • Biloma: collection near the biliary tree after biliary or hepatic surgery; usually simple unless infected.
  • Postoperative seroma: simple fluid that may contain recent postoperative gas and may require clinical correlation to distinguish from abscess.
  • Loculated ascites: minimal mass effect, no rim enhancement, and no internal gas.
  • Pancreatic pseudocyst: pancreatitis history or stigmata; pseudocapsule develops over weeks.
  • Hematoma: attenuation varies with age; acute clot is often high attenuation.
  • Retained oxidized cellulose (Surgicel): postoperative gas with little fluid and no discrete drainable collection.
  • Cystic or necrotic neoplasm can mimic abscess, especially when infectious clinical findings are absent.

🧬 Clinical / Path / Mechanism
  • Etiologies include enteric perforation, postoperative infection, bacteremia, and trauma.
  • RadPrimer describes pus within a peripheral fibrocapillary capsule; enteric abscesses are often polymicrobial.
  • Core notes that hepatic abscess commonly arises from bowel processes such as diverticulitis, appendicitis, Crohn disease, or bowel surgery; E. coli is the most common causative organism in that hepatic context.
  • Core also notes that perforated appendicitis can progress to abscess and that diverticulitis is complicated when abscess is present.

🛠️ Drainage / Management Pivots
  • Ideal percutaneous target: well-defined, encapsulated, fluid-filled abscess >3 cm with a safe catheter route.
  • Small abscesses, usually <3 cm, may be treated with antibiotics alone.
  • RadPrimer reports approximately 80% success for percutaneous abscess drainage with proper patient selection.
  • CT or ultrasound can guide transcutaneous, transgluteal, transrectal, or transvaginal drainage.
  • Most drain in 10-14 days; complex multiseptated collections or enteric fistulas may require weeks to months.
  • Catheter removal may be considered when output is <10 cc per shift or the cavity resolves on imaging.

⚠️ Pearls / Pitfalls
  • In postoperative patients, infected and noninfected collections can overlap; symptoms, labs, aspiration, timing, and follow-up may be required.
  • Do not require gas for diagnosis and do not label nondrainable phlegmon as abscess.
  • Gas after surgery is not automatically infection: Surgicel is a source-supported mimic.
  • Failure of presumed abscess drainage should raise concern for a cystic or necrotic neoplasm, as shown by the GIST mimic cases.

⭐ Super Summary
Think discrete rim-enhancing collection plus inflammatory environment, then ask: Is it truly drainable, what caused it, is gas meaningful in this context, and is there a source-supported mimic or contraindication to drainage?

column11: Why does a mature abdominal abscess typically show peripheral rim enhancement on contrast imaging?
column12: Localized infection produces central pus/infected fluid while the source describes a peripheral fibrocapillary capsule. The vascularized inflammatory capsule enhances after contrast, whereas the central fluid/pus does not enhance, creating the rim-enhancing collection pattern. This histology-to-imaging link is why a discrete enhancing capsule helps separate a mature abscess from ill-defined phlegmon.

column11: Why can internal gas appear within an abdominal abscess?
column12: The allowed source set gives two source-supported routes: gas can be produced by gas-forming infection, and gas can enter through communication with bowel. Therefore internal gas can strongly support infection when there has been no recent intervention, but it is not specific enough to ignore recent surgery/procedure or bowel fistulization.

column11: How can appendicitis progress to a periappendiceal abscess?
column12: Core describes luminal obstruction leading to venous congestion, mural ischemia, and bacterial translocation. If disease progresses to gangrenous or perforated appendicitis, infected material can localize adjacent to the appendix and form an abscess. Imaging therefore shifts from isolated appendiceal inflammation to a discrete periappendiceal collection in late complicated disease.

column11: Why can perforated diverticulitis produce a peridiverticular abscess?
column12: Diverticulitis involves inflammation of an obstructed diverticulum with microperforation. When contamination remains localized rather than freely disseminating, infected fluid can become walled off adjacent to the inflamed colon, producing the source-supported peridiverticular abscess pattern with a thick-walled collection abutting diseased bowel.

📚 Summary
  • Typical CT pattern: loculated or encapsulated low-density fluid collection with peripheral rim enhancement, with or without gas.
  • Internal gas is highly suspicious for infection when there has been no recent intervention, but gas may also reflect bowel communication.
  • Absence of gas does not exclude abscess; RadPrimer states that about half of abscesses contain gas.
  • Inflammatory support findings include adjacent fat stranding, edema, fascial thickening, and low-density parenchymal edema around intraparenchymal abscesses.
  • Use the term abscess for a discrete drainable collection; ill-defined inflammatory phlegmon is not equivalent to a drainable abscess.

🖼️ Key Imaging Findings
CT
  • Best overall imaging tool is contrast-enhanced CT.
  • Contents may have simple-fluid attenuation or be mildly hyperdense; rim enhancement and surrounding inflammatory change are major clues.
  • Hepatic pyogenic abscess may mimic metastasis as a ring-enhancing mass; reactive perilesional hyperenhancement may occur.
MR Imaging
  • Central fluid is low on T1 and high on T2, with peripheral rim enhancement; restricted diffusion with low ADC is often present.
  • Fat-saturated sequences can make surrounding edema conspicuous.
Ultrasound
  • Complex fluid may contain low-level echoes, debris, membranes, or septations; the center is avascular with peripheral hyperemia.
  • Gas may produce echogenic foci with ring-down artifact or dirty posterior acoustic shadowing.
  • In hepatic infection, an ill-defined altered-echogenicity phlegmon can evolve into a well-defined hypoechoic mature abscess with internal echoes.

  • Postoperative seroma: simple fluid that may contain recent postoperative gas and may require clinical correlation to distinguish from abscess.
  • Loculated ascites: minimal mass effect, no rim enhancement, and no internal gas.
  • Pancreatic pseudocyst: pancreatitis history or stigmata; pseudocapsule develops over weeks.

🧭 Abdominal Abscess

Abdominal abscess is a localized collection of pus or infected fluid. The central radiology task is to recognize a discrete drainable collection, distinguish it from phlegmon and sterile postoperative fluid, identify the source, and determine whether image-guided drainage is appropriate.
Source Basis: Core + RadPrimer + STATdx synthesis.

📚 Summary
  • Typical CT pattern: loculated or encapsulated low-density fluid collection with peripheral rim enhancement, with or without gas.
  • Internal gas is highly suspicious for infection when there has been no recent intervention, but gas may also reflect bowel communication.
  • Absence of gas does not exclude abscess; RadPrimer states that about half of abscesses contain gas.
  • Inflammatory support findings include adjacent fat stranding, edema, fascial thickening, and low-density parenchymal edema around intraparenchymal abscesses.
  • Use the term abscess for a discrete drainable collection; ill-defined inflammatory phlegmon is not equivalent to a drainable abscess.

🖼️ Key Imaging Findings
CT
  • Best overall imaging tool is contrast-enhanced CT.
  • Contents may have simple-fluid attenuation or be mildly hyperdense; rim enhancement and surrounding inflammatory change are major clues.
  • Hepatic pyogenic abscess may mimic metastasis as a ring-enhancing mass; reactive perilesional hyperenhancement may occur.
MR Imaging
  • Central fluid is low on T1 and high on T2, with peripheral rim enhancement; restricted diffusion with low ADC is often present.
  • Fat-saturated sequences can make surrounding edema conspicuous.
Ultrasound
  • Complex fluid may contain low-level echoes, debris, membranes, or septations; the center is avascular with peripheral hyperemia.
  • Gas may produce echogenic foci with ring-down artifact or dirty posterior acoustic shadowing.
  • In hepatic infection, an ill-defined altered-echogenicity phlegmon can evolve into a well-defined hypoechoic mature abscess with internal echoes.
